metaDescription: Six adjustable mandoline slicers compared on thickness range, guard design, stability and cleanup, with safety-first picks for handheld and countertop use.
introParagraphs: The word adjustable on a mandoline can mean three very different things: a dial that moves the blade deck, a few fixed notches you click between, or a set of built-in blades that you switch without handling the edge. All of them let you choose slice thickness, but they differ a great deal in how safe and stable the process feels.

We evaluated six adjustable mandolines using product specs and buyer feedback, focusing on thickness range, how the guard or food holder works, whether the base stays put, and how risky the blade is to clean and store. The lineup spans the Gramercy countertop slicer, the SupMaKin enclosed pusher design and four handheld models.

Mandolines are the tool that cuts more fingers than almost any other in the kitchen, so each pick notes its safety tradeoff plainly. The decision tables later in the guide connect your cooking habits to a named model. We do not claim hands-on testing; the notes reflect listings and reported experience.

products.name: Gramercy Mandoline Slicer With 12 Slice Settings
products.description:
The Gramercy is the most complete adjustable slicer in this group. A built-in dial offers 12 slice settings, from paper-thin to thick-cut, and a rotating blade cylinder switches between cutting styles without you ever unbolting or lifting a blade. The blade is a professional 4CR15 stainless steel, described as holding an edge.

Stability is a strength. A non-slip base with anti-slip feet keeps the slicer from creeping on the counter, which is the most common cause of accidents on lightweight models. The substantial build suggests a tool you set down and leave in place.

The cost of all that capability is space, because it takes more counter and cabinet room than the handheld OXO, Fullstar or Ibergrif. The blade is open, so you need a food holder or a cut-resistant glove every time, and the larger tool has more surfaces to clean. For a cook who slices potatoes, cucumbers and onions for the whole family, the precision justifies it.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want precise, repeatable thickness across many different vegetables.
pros: Thickness dial offers twelve settings in one tool
Rotating cylinder skips risky blade swaps
Anti-slip feet keep the base from creeping
Pro-grade 4CR15 blade holds a sharp edge
cons: Takes more counter and cabinet space than handhelds
Open blade needs extra care and a holder
Larger tool has more surfaces to clean

products.name: SupMaKin Safer Mandoline Slicer, 1-8 mm
products.description:
The SupMaKin takes the opposite approach from an open-blade mandoline. The blades are built in and enclosed, and you push a handle to move food through them, so fingertips never ride along the edge. Thickness is adjustable from 0.1 mm up to 8 mm, a wider range than most handheld models.

The stainless steel blades are described as heavy duty for hard produce, and the push handle replaces the habit of sliding food by hand. This design gives the most distance between hand and blade of anything in the lineup, which is why it appeals to cautious cooks and anyone with unsteady hands.

The tradeoffs are structural: the housing limits how large a whole vegetable you can feed, and the closed design is harder to inspect, so you need to rinse the inside right after use. Compared with the Gramercy it gives up the easy visual access and the 12 click settings, but gains safety. Compared with the OXO handheld, it needs more storage space.
products.bestFor: Safety-minded cooks who would rather never touch a blade.

Thickness runs from 0.1 mm to 8 mm

products.name: OXO Good Grips Handheld Mandoline Slicer

specList.label: Use
specList.value: Hooks over a bowl or rests on a board

products.description:
The OXO handheld slicer simplifies the adjustable idea down to three thickness settings: 1 mm, 2.5 mm and 4 mm. A large non-slip handle and a stable foot keep the tool steady, and it can hook over a bowl or slice straight onto a plate or board.

Its strength is how few things you have to think about. You pick one of three thicknesses, hold the big handle, and slice potatoes, cabbage, onions or cheese. The foot stops it sliding, and the hook means slices fall directly into the bowl, which cuts the awkward motions that lead to slips.

Three settings is also the limit, so it cannot match the Gramercy's 12 or the SupMaKin's 0.1 to 8 mm range. You also need a steady hand on the food while slicing, so pair it with a holder or glove. For salads, gratins and chips, three well chosen thicknesses are enough, and the compact size beats the countertop models in a small kitchen.
products.bestFor: Everyday slicing where a big comfortable handle matters more than thickness range.
pros: Large non-slip handle gives a confident hold
Stable foot keeps the slicer from sliding around
Hooks over a bowl for hands-free catching
Three thicknesses cover most slicing jobs
cons: Needs a steady hand on the food while slicing

products.name: Fullstar Handheld Mandoline Slicer And Julienne Cutter
products.description:
The Fullstar handheld slicer adds one more setting than the OXO, giving four thickness options at 1, 2, 3 and 4 mm, plus a built-in julienne blade that turns the same tool into a matchstick cutter. The hand guard has stainless steel tips, described as offering better grip than flimsy plastic ones.

That guard detail matters because a holder that skids off produce is no protection at all. Metal tips bite into the food, keep fingers back and give a more stable push stroke. The 2-in-1 layout also saves a second gadget, which is useful if you make slaw, fries or garnishes.

It still has the weakness of any handheld: the user supplies the stability. There is no listed non-slip base, unlike the Gramercy, and its range tops out at 4 mm, well short of the SupMaKin at 8 mm. For thin slicing and julienne in a small drawer, it is the best handheld in the group for its guard and its extra setting.
products.bestFor: Salads and slaw where thin slices and julienne cuts are both needed.
pros: Four settings from 1 mm to 4 mm
Stainless steel guard tips grip produce
Built-in julienne blade adds a second cut
Compact handheld size stores easily
cons: No non-slip base is named in the listing

products.name: Ibergrif Handheld Adjustable Vegetable Slicer
products.description:
The Ibergrif is a handheld slicer built around three adjustable thicknesses, a food holder and a blade safety lock. The stainless steel blade is sharp, and the lock secures the edge for storage and cleaning, which is where many accidental cuts happen after the cooking is over.

The included holder keeps fingertips at a distance from the blade, and a non-slip design supports a steadier stroke. The listing frames it as meal prep for salads, chips and small kitchen use, and it is compact enough for a small drawer.

The lighter build leaves more of the control to your own hands, and the holder adapts poorly to odd-shaped produce. Against the OXO handheld, it has the same three thicknesses but adds the blade lock. Against the SupMaKin, it needs more attention while cutting. If you want a low-footprint option that locks the blade away, it is a practical choice.
products.bestFor: Small kitchens that want a lockable blade and a compact slicer.

Includes a food holder for fingertip distance
Three thickness settings suit salads and chips
Compact enough for a small drawer
cons: Lighter build leaves more work to your own control

products.name: PrepSolutions Adjust-A-Slice Mandoline Slicer
products.description:
The PrepSolutions Adjust-A-Slice is positioned around one idea, adjustable slicing thickness, for all your prep needs. The listing is short on detail: it confirms a single green mandoline in the box and the adjustable thickness feature, without giving a range, blade material or guard description.

That limited information is itself a data point. With the Gramercy listing 12 settings and a 4CR15 blade, or the Fullstar listing 1 to 4 mm and steel guard tips, this pick leaves more to assume. The adjustable design means you can pick thicker or thinner cuts without swapping blades, which is the main benefit here.

For that reason it works best as a straightforward, low commitment slicer for someone who values simplicity and is willing to check the dimensions before buying. Confirm whether a holder is included and how the base grips the counter, since the brief does not say. If safety features matter most, the SupMaKin or Ibergrif document theirs more clearly.
products.bestFor: Basic adjustable slicing for cooks who prefer a minimal tool.
pros: Adjustable thickness covers different prep jobs
Single unit with no extra blades to store
Simple hand-operated design is easy to learn
cons: Listing gives few specs on blade or guard
Thickness range is not stated in the listing

buyingCriteria.explanation: Adjustable should come with a stated range so you know the tool matches your recipes. The Gramercy gives 12 settings, the SupMaKin runs 0.1 to 8 mm, the Fullstar offers 1 to 4 mm in four steps, and the OXO and Ibergrif each provide three. For chips and gratin you want 2 to 3 mm, while paper-thin cucumber needs under 1 mm. Choose the model whose range includes your most frequent cut with room to spare.

The guard sits between your hand and the blade, so its quality is your first safety measure. The Fullstar uses stainless steel guard tips for grip, the Ibergrif includes a holder, and the SupMaKin removes the issue with built-in blades and a push handle. Many holders grip poorly on small or soft items, so use a cut-resistant glove as a second layer when slicing the last inch.

A slicer that slides mid-stroke is dangerous. The Gramercy uses anti-slip feet and a heavy build, and the OXO has a stable foot that also hooks over a bowl. Lighter handhelds depend on how firmly you press on a board. Always place a damp towel under any unit without a rubber base before you begin.

Open blades are fast and clean-cutting but demand respect. The Gramercy uses a 4CR15 stainless blade on a rotating cylinder, so changing cut style does not require lifting a blade. The SupMaKin has built-in stainless blades with no exposure. The Ibergrif adds a blade lock for storage, which cuts accident risk during drawer storage.

Most mandoline injuries happen at the sink or in the drawer. Wash blades with a brush, never a sponge pressed against the edge, and rinse enclosed designs like the SupMaKin straight after use so food does not dry inside. The Gramercy has more surfaces to wash than the handhelds, and the handheld OXO and Fullstar slide into a drawer far more easily.

Match the tool to what you slice. The SupMaKin's housing limits whole vegetable size, handhelds like the OXO suit potatoes, cabbage and onions, and the Gramercy handles larger items with a stable deck. Soft tomatoes need a very sharp blade and short steady strokes. If you slice big squash or watermelon rind, a countertop deck is easier than a handheld.

howWeEvaluated.title: Adjustment range
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared documented thickness ranges and steps. The Gramercy leads with 12 settings, the SupMaKin spans 0.1 to 8 mm, the Fullstar offers four steps from 1 to 4 mm, and the OXO and Ibergrif offer three. The PrepSolutions listing states no range, which counted against it.

howWeEvaluated.title: Safety design
howWeEvaluated.description: Based on product specs, we weighed guards, holders, blade locks and enclosed blades. The SupMaKin hides its blades, the Ibergrif locks its blade, the Fullstar uses steel guard tips, and the Gramercy relies on a rotating cylinder. Designs reducing blade contact scored highest.

howWeEvaluated.title: Stability
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked for anti-slip feet, hooks and non-slip handles, such as the Gramercy feet and the OXO stable foot. Handhelds without a listed base lost points.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cutting performance
howWeEvaluated.description: We read blade material and buyer feedback on evenness and hard produce. The 4CR15 stainless blade on the Gramercy and the heavy-duty stainless blades on the SupMaKin were credited for hard vegetables.

howWeEvaluated.title: Storage and cleanup
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared size, parts and cleaning risk. Handhelds like the OXO, Fullstar and Ibergrif store in a drawer, while the Gramercy and SupMaKin need more room. Lineup positioning: Gramercy leads on precision, SupMaKin on safety, OXO on grip.

faq.q: What does adjustable mean on a mandoline?
faq.a: It means you can change slice thickness, but the method varies. The Gramercy uses a dial with 12 settings, the OXO offers 1, 2.5 and 4 mm, and the SupMaKin adjusts from 0.1 to 8 mm. Look for stated numbers rather than the word alone.

Yes, because the blade is very sharp and the food gets small near the end. A guard, a cut-resistant glove and a stable base reduce the risk. Stop slicing when the produce gets short rather than pushing your fingertips through.

Generally, since the SupMaKin keeps blades enclosed and uses a push handle. It still needs careful cleaning, and the housing limits food size. Safer does not mean risk free, so rinse promptly and store it out of reach.

faq.q: What thickness should I use for potato chips?
faq.a: Most cooks use about 1 to 2 mm for crisp chips and about 3 to 4 mm for gratin. The Fullstar offers 1, 2, 3 and 4 mm, and the OXO offers 1, 2.5 and 4 mm. A dial slicer like the Gramercy lets you fine tune.

faq.q: How do I clean a mandoline safely?
faq.a: Use a brush or a long handled tool and rinse under running water, keeping fingers off the edge. Never wipe a blade with a sponge. Lock the blade if the model has a lock, like the Ibergrif, before storage.

faq.q: Do I need a cut-resistant glove?
faq.a: It is a strong idea for any open-blade model. Gloves let you keep slicing past the point where the holder stops gripping. They are not a substitute for care, but they add a real second layer.

faq.q: Can a handheld replace a countertop mandoline?
faq.a: For salads, chips and small batches, yes. The OXO, Fullstar and Ibergrif are enough for most households. For large volumes or big vegetables, the Gramercy deck or the SupMaKin housing is easier.
